details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: The priority list contains 'Throughput' three times, but no KPI named 'Throughput' exists in the contract — should the priority order be ['resource_efficiency', 'operator_fatigue', 'noise_level'], or is raw throughput (units/hour) a separate objective that needs to be added alongside resource_efficiency?
flags.resolution: Priority order is corrected to ['resource_efficiency', 'operator_fatigue', 'noise_level'] in that sequence; no standalone throughput KPI is added unless the manager confirms otherwise.

flags.question: Resource efficiency is set to maximise with no upper bound or target ceiling — should a maximum improvement cap be specified (e.g. no more than 20–25% above the prior-shift baseline) to prevent the optimiser from consuming all available constraint slack in fatigue and noise simultaneously just to squeeze marginal efficiency gains?
flags.resolution: Efficiency is maximised subject only to the existing hard constraints (fatigue ≤ 0.4, noise ≤ 80 dB) with no additional efficiency ceiling applied; the optimiser may drive both constraints to their limits.

flags.question: The contract scope is 'single_shift' but no concrete shift duration is defined — is this an 8-hour standard shift, a 10-hour extended shift, or a 12-hour shift? The answer changes the permissible fatigue accumulation rate per hour and the cumulative noise dose ceiling (e.g. 80 dB for 8 h vs. a lower equivalent limit for 10–12 h under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.95).
flags.resolution: Shift duration is assumed to be 8 hours; fatigue and noise thresholds are interpreted relative to an 8-hour exposure window with no overtime extension.

flags.question: Maximising resource efficiency typically requires higher cycle rates or eliminated idle time, which accelerates operator fatigue toward the 0.4 hard limit. If fatigue reaches 0.4 before the shift ends, should the optimiser hold the current pace (capping further efficiency gains), or may it insert job-rotation or mandatory micro-breaks to reset fatigue and resume higher-efficiency operation?
flags.resolution: When fatigue hits 0.4 the work rate is throttled to hold fatigue at the boundary for the remainder of the shift; no job-rotation or break-insertion logic is activated unless separately configured.

flags.question: Is the 80 dB limit measured at the operator's ear (personal occupational exposure), as a continuous ambient average across the production floor, or at the machine boundary? The feasible operating envelope can differ by 4–8 dB depending on measurement point, which could make the constraint either easily satisfied or binding at normal production rates.
flags.resolution: Noise is evaluated as a continuous A-weighted ambient average at the nearest occupied operator workstation, consistent with the 'continuous_ambient_A_weighted_dB_averaged_over_shift' assumption already declared in the contract.

details.trigger: Contract deployed; system enters autonomous monitoring

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Schedule S1 was authored assuming approximately 46 UPH during Phase 2. Actual throughput has settled at 40.7 UPH — an 11.5% shortfall. Because DeadlineGap is computed as remaining capacity minus remaining demand across the shift horizon, a sustained UPH deficit of this magnitude directly erodes the buffer. Each hour of under-production compounds the gap: at 40.7 vs 46 UPH, the schedule accumulates roughly 5.3 units of unrecovered shortfall per hour, which at Phase 2 mid-point has collapsed the deadline margin to near-zero.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately re-sequence remaining Phase 2 lots to prioritize highest-priority SKUs; evaluate authorizing a temporary 5–8% robot speed increase on non-fatigue-critical stations to recover throughput, and flag to shift supervisor for potential overtime extension if margin cannot be recovered within the next 20 minutes.

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Operator fatigue index assumed stable at ~0.25 baseline
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Contract assumptions modeled operator fatigue at approximately 0.25 for this phase. Observed fatigue_index of 0.3501 represents a 40% elevation above baseline, consistent with operator absence causing workload redistribution onto remaining staff. Elevated fatigue degrades manual task cycle times and increases micro-error rates, which in turn causes micro-stoppages and rework loops. These losses are not individually large but aggregate into a measurable UPH drag — the observed 40.7 UPH shortfall is partially attributable to this fatigue-induced inefficiency. The fatigue trajectory also suggests further degradation is likely in the remaining phase window, meaning the deadline gap will widen unless intervention occurs.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Redistribute workload immediately by rotating any available standby operator or cross-trained technician to the highest-fatigue stations; reduce manual handling cycle targets by 5% to prevent fatigue-index crossing the 0.40 critical threshold, and log operator absence as a root-cause event for post-shift contract deviation report.

l4_llm_attributions.assumption: Energy consumption assumed at ~360 kWh for Phase 2 cycle volume
l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Energy consumption at 401 kWh is running 11.4% above the assumed Phase 2 budget of approximately 360 kWh. Elevated energy without a corresponding throughput gain indicates system inefficiency — likely caused by robots operating at higher-than-nominal force or speed to compensate for throughput shortfall, or by unplanned idle-running during micro-stoppages caused by fatigue events. This inefficiency loop (push speed → higher energy → no throughput gain → deadline gap persists) suggests the throughput deficit cannot be solved purely by increasing machine intensity without also resolving the fatigue-driven bottleneck.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Audit robot duty cycles at stations with highest energy draw; if idle-running is detected during fatigue-related pauses, implement automatic standby mode to recover energy budget and avoid thermal stress accumulation that could trigger unplanned maintenance during Phase 3.

details.rationale: No feasible candidate exists in the non-dominated front. Returning 'balanced-aggressive' (highest V/R = 0.481) as a fallback; manual review required before deployment.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Fatigue index of 0.5709 exceeds the 0.40 limit by ~43%. The human_cycle_rate_multiplier is the direct driver of operator fatigue: higher cycle rates compress recovery time and increase cumulative musculoskeletal load. Assuming roughly linear fatigue scaling, the effective base fatigue at multiplier=1.0 is approximately 0.5709/1.15 ≈ 0.496. To reach the 0.40 ceiling, the multiplier must fall to approximately 0.40/0.496 ≈ 0.806; rounding conservatively to 0.80 provides a small safety margin. This is the binding constraint and should be fixed first before tuning robot speeds.

Noise at 83.2 dB exceeds the 80.0 dB limit by 3.2 dB. Robot mechanical noise is the primary controllable acoustic source. Reducing r1 speed from 0.90 to 0.80 (an 11% reduction) lowers its acoustic power contribution; combined with an equivalent r2 reduction, the two-robot aggregate power drops by roughly 50%, corresponding to approximately 3 dB of noise reduction. Targeting 0.80 rather than a smaller cut ensures the combined robot reduction closes the full 3.2 dB gap without requiring a third intervention.

Noise reduction from r1 alone is insufficient to close the full 3.2 dB gap. Applying the same 0.90→0.80 reduction to r2 symmetrically brings the combined robot acoustic output down by approximately 50% relative to the current operating point. Symmetric speed reduction also avoids introducing robot-to-robot throughput imbalance that could create upstream buffer starvation or downstream pileup. The resulting noise level is estimated at ~79.5–80.0 dB, just at or below the 80 dB limit.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 25.0% demand surge has rendered the current production schedule infeasible under the active human-centric constraints. Two violations are present: (1) FatigueIndex reached 0.5709, exceeding the 0.40 ceiling by a margin of +0.1709 — representing a 42.7% overage that poses meaningful ergonomic and safety risk to workers; (2) Ambient Noise reached 83.2 dB, exceeding the 80.0 dB limit by 3.2 dB — a level associated with hearing strain over sustained exposure. Both violations stem directly from the intensity and duration of the expanded schedule required to absorb the demand spike. No feasible schedule exists that simultaneously satisfies full demand and both constraints at their current thresholds. Immediate managerial decision is required to select a remediation path before production can resume.
options: Option 1 — Workforce Augmentation and Load Redistribution (Recommended)
Option 2 — Partial Fulfillment with Expedited External Sourcing
Option 3 — Time-Limited Constraint Relaxation with Enhanced Compensatory Controls (Last Resort)

details.trigger: Manager decision received; system resumes autonomous execution

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with dual constraint violations (FatigueIndex at 100%, Noise at 80%) under a +25% demand surge indicates the current policy is fundamentally misaligned. MICRO parameter tweaks cannot resolve a 100% fatigue violation — small speed adjustments of ±5% would likely worsen fatigue if speeds increase to meet demand, or fail to meet demand if speeds decrease. Prior learning strongly corroborates this: both prior similar situations rejected S2 (the current or similar policy family) and accepted S3, indicating a policy family switch (S2→S3) consistently resolves this disturbance pattern. The demand surge magnitude (+25%) is substantial but not so catastrophic as to require full L1-L2 replanning.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience unanimously (2/2) shows S2-family policies fail and S3-family policies succeed under this disturbance pattern; MESO switch from S2→S3 is the evidence-backed minimal intervention.

experience_synthesis.pattern: demand_surge: S2 is deterministically infeasible (hard constraint violations on Fatigue and Noise); S3 is the consistently viable adaptation policy
experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is rejected deterministically across all observed demand_surge attempts due to hard ergonomic and acoustic constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB), indicating it should be pruned from the candidate set for this disturbance type regardless of other conditions. S3 succeeds in both attempts with narrow throughput variance (~42.3–42.6 UPH) and a declining deadline_gap_pct trend (32.2 → 28.8), suggesting improving adaptation quality over repetitions. The deterministic nature of S2 rejection raises confidence in that negative finding above what a 2-sample size would normally warrant, while the positive S3 finding remains tentative pending more observations.
